strengths: The proposed LaRI representation is conceptually clear and useful: it extends depth/point-map prediction to a fixed set of depth-ordered ray-surface intersections, allowing single-view methods to represent unseen and self-occluded geometry rather than only the first visible surface.

The ray stopping index formulation is simple, well motivated, and empirically better than direct binary mask prediction in the ablation (Table 6), enforcing the ordered structure of valid intersections.

The paper provides a substantial data-generation pipeline combining Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, Blender, and PyTorch3D, with cleaning steps and coordination between rendering engines. This pipeline and the promised public benchmark are potentially valuable to the community.

Object-level experiments are promising: with view-aligned ground truth, LaRI outperforms SF3D, SPAR3D, and TRELLIS on FS@0.02, and with canonical ground truth it is close to TRELLIS while using far less training data and far fewer parameters.

Scene-level results demonstrate a genuine capability that conventional depth/point-map methods lack: reasoning about unseen surfaces in one feed-forward pass, with qualitative depth-ordered layer visualizations supporting the claim.
The paper includes useful ablations on number of layers, pretrained weights, mask prediction strategy, and efficiency comparisons, and it gives an honest limitations discussion.
The presentation is generally strong, with clear motivation, problem formulation, and illustrative figures.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol for the object-level view-aligned comparison is not fully clear. LaRI is intrinsically camera-aligned, while the competing generative methods likely require registration even in the view-aligned setting; if so, the comparison may unfairly favor LaRI. The paper should specify exactly how every baseline is aligned under each GT setting.

Several directly related occlusion-revealing/single-view geometry methods are not compared experimentally, especially Slice3D (multi-slice occlusion-revealing reconstruction), amodal depth methods, and KYN-style methods. Dismissing them because they may require interactions is not sufficient for all; at least Slice3D appears highly relevant and should be benchmarked.

The scene-level overall FS@0.05 is clearly worse than MoGe (0.590 vs. 0.668), and visible-surface metrics are also worse. The claim that scene-level performance is comparable to large models is therefore overstated; it is competitive on CD/FS@0.1 but not uniformly comparable.

The data filtering heuristics for Objaverse may bias training toward objects whose intersections are mostly in the first two layers, potentially limiting the method's ability to learn complex multi-layer, thin, transparent, or highly self-occluded structures.

The mask/stopping-index prediction quality is only moderate in the ablation (mIoU around 0.55-0.56, DICE around 0.59-0.64). Since hidden geometry is inherently ambiguous from a single image, deterministic regression may be unreliable in high-occlusion cases, as the limitations section acknowledges.

Architecture and efficiency reporting is somewhat ambiguous: the method appears to use separate ViT-Large backbones for LaRI prediction and mask prediction, but Table 5 reports only about 314M parameters and 31.5 ms inference time. It should be clarified whether both networks are included and what the end-to-end cost is.
No real-world object-level evaluation is provided; the object-level benchmark uses rendered images from GSO. This limits evidence for real-image generalization.
There is no broader-impact or ethics discussion, particularly given the use of real-world scanned indoor data and potential privacy concerns.

strengths: The core representation (layered ray intersections / layered point maps) is conceptually clean and clearly positioned relative to depth maps, point maps, NeRF, and occupancy/grid representations. Framing it as the 'reverse' of LDI generation is a nice conceptual handle.

The ray stopping index formulation (Sec. 3.3, Eq. 4-5) is an elegant and sensible way to enforce the ordering constraint of valid intersections, and replacing L uncorrelated binary masks with a single ordinal index is well-motivated by the structure of the problem.

The data construction effort is a genuine contribution: filtering random internal structures in Objaverse, splitting multi-room 3D-FRONT houses into rooms, subsampling ScanNet++, and coordinating Blender and PyTorch3D to render LaRI ground truth is non-trivial engineering that the community would benefit from if released.
Efficiency results (Table 5) are strong: ~314M params and ~31.5ms versus TRELLIS (1795M, ~734ms), with a clear practical advantage from view-aligned outputs that avoid registration/post-processing.

The view-aligned output is a real practical benefit for downstream use (robotics/VR), and the qualitative figures (Fig. 3-4) support the claim that the method is deterministic and faithful to the input image, which is a meaningful contrast to generative baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim (unseen-geometry reasoning) is supported mainly by an evaluation setting that structurally favors the proposed method. In Table 1 the method is *worse* than TRELLIS under the method-agnostic Canonical GT (CD 0.029 vs 0.027; FS@0.02 0.601 vs 0.611) and only wins under View-aligned GT, where a camera-aligned predictor has an inherent advantage over methods requiring ICP registration. The headline 'comparable/better' claim therefore rests on the favorable protocol.

Evaluation uses the ground-truth mask to remove invalid regions ('we sample 10,000 points for all methods and use the GT mask to remove invalid regions'). Since producing the valid-intersection mask via the ray stopping index is one of the paper's two core components, bypassing it at test time undercuts the evidence that the full pipeline works; the main metric does not actually measure mask quality.

Scene-level evidence is weak. On visible surfaces the method is substantially worse than MoGe (CD 0.057 vs 0.035; FS@0.05 0.589 vs 0.786), and the 'overall' win is marginal in CD (0.059 vs 0.063) and a loss in FS@0.1 (0.825 vs 0.836). The claim of 'competitive performance' is a thin margin driven by the unseen term, while degrading the visible term that matters most in practice.

Amodal depth estimation [39] is the most directly related single-view unseen-surface method and is dismissed in prose ('requires estimated masks... human intervention') without any quantitative comparison. Given that this is the closest prior work, its omission weakens the empirical positioning of the contribution.

Novelty is limited relative to the acknowledged prior art. Layered depth images and depth peeling already define the multi-layer ray-intersection representation; what is added is supervision of a 2D network to regress it plus the stopping-index head. These are reasonable but incremental; the paper's own framing ('reverse LDI') concedes the representational idea is not new.

Table 6 reports binary segmentation mIoU of 0.091 vs 0.560 for ray stopping index. Such a large gap for a plain per-layer binary head is surprising and unexplained; if it is a training/implementation artifact of the baseline rather than a property of the formulation, the ablation is not informative. At minimum the baseline's training protocol should be described.

The 'unified object- and scene-level' claim overstates the method: separate models are trained for the two domains (Sec. 4.3), so unification is only at the representation level, not at the model level.

Presentation and consistency issues: Table 5 cites MoGe as [73] (should be [72]) and uses duplicate 'Ours' rows for two scenarios without clear labeling; the parameter-reduction ratio is quoted as 17%, 17.5%, and computes to ~19% (341/1795) across the text; Table 2's 'Ours' vs 'Ours*' distinction is hard to parse and the sampling protocol differs from competitors, complicating fair reading.

Reproducibility is promised but not demonstrated: datasets, evaluation scripts, and the Blender/PyTorch3D coordination pipeline are 'to be released,' so the central data-generation and registration-free evaluation claims cannot currently be verified. The 'at least 30% of the pixels containing an unseen structure' criterion for SCRREAM frames is also underspecified.

The representation has an acknowledged intrinsic ceiling (reduced point density on surfaces parallel to rays and between layers; Sec. 5 and Fig. 5). Since the method can only place points where camera rays intersect surfaces, it cannot represent geometry not intersected by rays (interior structure, tangent surfaces), which limits the 'complete' modeling claim; the suggested remedy is post-processing, not the model.

strengths: Introduces a novel layered ray intersection (LaRI) representation that models multiple ray-surface intersections as depth-ordered layered point maps, extending standard depth and point-map representations toward unseen geometry reasoning in a view-aligned and compact manner.

The overall formulation is technically sound: LaRI is predicted as a 2D regression task with scale-shift alignment, and the ray stopping index provides an elegant way to enforce ordered valid intersection layers instead of predicting independent binary masks.

The paper targets an important and useful problem, unifying object-level and scene-level single-view geometric reasoning with a single feed-forward pass and avoiding the expensive per-point sampling, iterative inference, or manual pose/mask conditioning of many prior methods.

Efficiency results are strong: LaRI reports 314M parameters and 31.5 ms inference, substantially lighter and faster than generative baselines such as TRELLIS, while achieving competitive object-level accuracy with far less training data.

Object-level view-aligned results are convincing and favorable, with improvements over SF3D, SPAR3D, and TRELLIS under camera-aligned evaluation, and the comparison against TRELLIS using 4% of its training data and 17.5% of its parameters is notable.

The data construction pipeline is a substantial contribution, combining Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, and ScanNet++ with cleaning, room splitting, filtering, and Blender/PyTorch3D coordination for LaRI renderings.

Ablations are informative: layer count, pretrained weights, and ray stopping index versus binary mask prediction are studied, and the ray stopping index formulation clearly improves mask prediction over direct binary segmentation.
The limitations section is honest about low point density for rays parallel to surfaces, sensitivity to limited observations, and limited data diversity, which is appropriate for the claims.
weaknesses: The central claim of modeling all ray intersections is only approximated by a fixed layer count, typically L=5. For complex scenes or objects with many overlapping surfaces, this representation is incomplete, and the paper does not demonstrate adaptive or robust behavior when the true number of intersections exceeds L; this limits the strength of the completeness claim.

Scene-level evaluation is not fully convincing for the strongest claims. Although LaRI improves overall Chamfer distance slightly over MoGe, its overall F-score at 0.05 is lower than MoGe (0.590 vs. 0.668), and its visible-surface performance is much worse than MoGe (FS@0.05 0.589 vs. 0.786). The abstract's "overall scores comparable" phrasing understates this discrepancy and needs more careful support.

Evaluation fairness is questionable in places. View-aligned ground truth naturally advantages LaRI's camera-aligned output, while canonical evaluation requires ICP for competing methods; the paper does not fully isolate how much of the gain comes from representation versus evaluation protocol. Scale-shift alignment and mask usage also need clearer standardization across baselines.

Important unseen-geometry baselines are discussed but not quantitatively compared, including KYN, AmodalDepth, and NeRF-based/coordinate-querying methods. CUT3R is evaluated only as iter-5 for reference, which is not a strong enough comparison for the broad claim of geometric reasoning about unseen surfaces.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper promises to release data and evaluation scripts, but no code or pretrained weights are mentioned, and critical details are missing: exact filtering thresholds, decoder architectures, ray stopping index network design, loss weighting, and baseline alignment procedures. This makes independent reproduction difficult.

Several presentation and reference errors reduce clarity and credibility. For example, ViT-Large is cited as [75], which is an SSIM image-quality paper, not the ViT paper; Figure 4's caption cites [16] for SCRREAM although [16] is GSO; Table 5 confuses DUSt3R/MoGe references and contains a typo ('DUSi3R'). These should be corrected.

The training data comparison is ambiguous: the abstract claims 4% of TRELLIS's training data, but the paper reports 16K objects versus 500K objects, and also 190K rendered images; the exact basis of the 4% claim should be clarified.

No error bars, repeated runs, or statistical significance tests are reported. Given the small margins in some object-level canonical comparisons and the mixed scene-level metrics, uncertainty quantification would strengthen the empirical claims.

The ray stopping index mask prediction is far from perfect (mIoU around 0.56), and errors in stopping index directly corrupt the valid point cloud. The paper does not analyze sensitivity to mask errors or how such errors affect downstream reconstruction and evaluation.

The work is mostly limited to indoor and object-level data; it does not address outdoor scenes or large-scale environments, despite claiming potential for large scenes. This restricts the practical scope of the method.

The deterministic regression may produce degraded or implausible geometry under heavy occlusion or limited observation, as acknowledged in the limitations, but no mitigation or uncertainty-aware variant is proposed or evaluated.

strengths: Introduces LaRI, a layered point-map representation that models all camera-ray/surface intersections in depth order, extending depth/point-map representations to occluded surfaces. The ray-stopping index is a simple and effective way to enforce valid consecutive intersection layers.

Constructs a nontrivial annotation pipeline and benchmark across five public datasets, covering synthetic and real object/scene data. This is a useful community contribution for evaluating visible and unseen geometry.

Experiments are broad: object-level canonical and view-aligned reconstruction, scene-level visible/unseen/overall reconstruction, ablations on layer number, pre-training, mask prediction, and efficiency. Results support the utility of multi-layer prediction, e.g., scene unseen CD 0.076 vs. CUT3R 0.271 on 3D-FRONT, and ray-stopping mIoU 0.560 vs. binary mask 0.091.

Efficiency is convincingly better than large generative object reconstruction methods (about 620M params/51.5 ms vs. SPAR3D 2026M/904.8 ms and TRELLIS 1795M/733.7 ms), and comparable to feed-forward scene methods.
The limitations are discussed honestly, including low point density on ray-parallel surfaces and limited observations, and the impact statement encourages uncertainty-aware deployment.
View-aligned output simplifies downstream RGB-D/3D integration, and quantitative gains under view-aligned ground truth are shown.
weaknesses: The central claim of one feed-forward pass is imprecise: producing the final valid point cloud requires a separate ray-stopping-index ViT-Large network, so the full pipeline involves two feed-forward networks/passes. This should be corrected or explicitly framed per model.

The main 3D comparisons use the ground-truth ray-intersection mask for evaluation, so they do not measure end-to-end accuracy with the predicted stopping index. This likely overstates practical reconstruction quality. An end-to-end evaluation using predicted masks should be reported.

Novelty over layered depth images/depth peeling in graphics is incremental: the core representation adapts LDI-style layers to supervised point-map regression, with the ray-stopping index and datasets as the main technical additions.

Object-level canonical results do not beat TRELLIS (CD 0.029 vs. 0.027; FS@0.02 0.601 vs. 0.611), so the abstract's higher-accuracy claim needs qualification and should be scoped to view-aligned/efficiency settings.

Presentation and technical issues remain: ViT-Large is cited as Wang et al. (2004) multiple times, likely meaning Dosovitskiy et al. (2020); Table 6 duplicates the Ours rows; and the sampling procedure is unclear when predicted point counts differ from the 100k GT points.

The scene-level unseen-geometry comparison is limited: only CUT3R (iter-5) is a direct unseen baseline, while other occluded-scene methods are excluded because they require extra inputs. The completeness claim is therefore not fully benchmarked.

Fixed L=5 may truncate geometry, and layer-coverage plots are only shown for Objaverse/GSO, not for the scene datasets used in unseen evaluation. The effect of predicted mask errors on recall/completeness is not fully analyzed.

Reproducibility is only partial: the annotation pipeline and models are promised for release, but code/data are not yet available, and the coordinate-conversion details are nontrivial and time-consuming.
Some metrics are under-specified, including the scale/normalization of F-score thresholds and Chamfer distance units, which may affect comparability across methods.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: single-view reasoning about occluded/unseen geometry is practically relevant, and reformulating it as multi-layer ray-intersection regression with view-aligned output is a clean, intuitive framing.

A genuinely useful data contribution: an annotation/rendering pipeline that converts 5 public datasets (Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, SCRREAM, GSO) into multi-layer point-map ground truth, with careful discussion of cross-engine coordinate conventions (Sec. A.1).

Empirical breadth and ablations are unusually thorough: number of layers (Table 4), pretrained weights including DINOv2/v3 vs MoGe (Table 5), mask strategy (Table 7), separate vs shared encoders (Table 8), per-layer accuracy (Table 9), and point-map vs depth+focal outputs (Table 10).
Efficiency is convincingly demonstrated: one feed-forward pass with ~314M (point-map model) / 620M (with stopping-index model) parameters and 31-52 ms, far below SF3D/SPAR3D/TRELLIS (Table 6).
Limitations are honestly discussed (layer-parallel density loss, inaccuracy under limited context, synthetic-to-real domain gap), and an appropriate deployment/ethics statement is included.
The ray-stopping-index formulation (argmax over L+1 logits, Eq. 6/7) yields a simple and interpretable alternative to per-layer binary mask regression.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the paper's framing. Layered depth images (Shade et al., 1998) already represent multi-layer ray intersections; the network is an off-the-shelf ViT-Large encoder plus DPT-style heads with L heads, and the training loss is standard scale-shift-aligned Euclidean regression. The only substantive technical element is the stopping-index regression, which is a small addition.

The central 'outperforms existing methods' claim is overstated. In canonical-GT object evaluation (Table 2) LaRI is actually worse than TRELLIS on every metric (CD 0.029 vs 0.027; FS@0.02 0.601 vs 0.611), yet the abstract/text present the method as delivering 'notable improvements over existing methods' and 'higher reconstruction accuracy'. This is a framing-vs-evidence mismatch, not merely a limitations issue.

Scene-level comparisons are not a fair fight and are not framed as such. LaRI's scene model is trained in-domain on 3D-FRONT/ScanNet++, while it is compared against zero-shot foundation models (MoGe, DUSt3R, DepthPro) that were never trained to output multi-layer intersections. The 'best in unseen' result is largely true by construction since depth/point-map baselines cannot represent occluded layers at all, and no zero-shot variant of LaRI is reported to isolate the data advantage.

The visible-surface tradeoff is understated. On SCRREAM, LaRI's visible FS@0.05 is 0.589 vs MoGe's 0.786, i.e., LaRI is substantially worse where the two methods are directly comparable; the 'competitive or better overall' claim rests mainly on the trivially-zero unseen term of the baselines. The enormous gap between 3D-FRONT unseen FS@0.05 (0.739) and SCRREAM unseen FS@0.05 (0.494) also suggests the synthetic benchmark is inflated by repetitive 3D-FRONT room statistics, which is not analyzed.

The core mask-prediction ablation (Table 7) is unconvincing. A binary-segmentation baseline reaching only mIoU 0.091 / DICE 0.154 suggests the baseline is under-trained or evaluated with an unfavorable protocol; the stopping-index result (mIoU 0.560) is also low in absolute terms. Since the stopping index is one of only two stated technical contributions, this weak baseline undermines the claim.

Evaluation protocol choices make the numbers hard to interpret. Reconstruction metrics use a per-scene global scale + z-shift alignment (Eq. 4) and filter predictions with the GT mask ('we use the GT mask for evaluation'), which means the learned mask network does not affect the headline reconstruction numbers. The interaction between mask error and reported geometry metrics is never quantified.

Presentation and reference hygiene problems: ViT is cited as 'Wang et al., 2004' (which is the SSIM paper) in Sec. 3.2 and 3.3; DINOv3 is cited inconsistently (Siméoni 2025 in text vs Oquab 2023 in Table 5); Table 6 lists 'Ours' twice and cites MoGe as Wang et al., 2024a while elsewhere it is Wang et al., 2025c; there are grammatical errors ('It inferences of all ray intersections...'). These are minor individually but collectively signal insufficient care.

Reproducibility is deferred: code and the data-generation pipeline are promised but not available, and the pipeline depends on multiple large, license-restricted datasets and two graphics engines, making independent replication non-trivial.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: complete single-view 3D geometry reasoning, including occluded surfaces, with a clear layered representation inspired by layered depth images.

The method is simple, efficient, and feed-forward: it predicts multiple ray-surface intersection layers in one pass and avoids iterative NeRF/grid queries or additional pose/mask queries. Efficiency comparisons show competitive parameter counts and inference times against large generative and feed-forward baselines.

The ray stopping index is a sensible and effective formulation for identifying valid intersections. It naturally enforces depth ordering, and the ablation against direct binary mask regression shows clear segmentation improvements (Table 7).

The data/benchmark contribution is substantial: the authors construct annotations for five public datasets (Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, SCRREAM, GSO) and provide an annotation pipeline, which addresses the lack of supervision/evaluation data for layered ray intersections.

The evaluation is broad: object-level canonical and view-aligned GSO, scene-level 3D-FRONT and SCRREAM, visible/unseen/overall partitions, and ablations on number of layers, pretrained weights, output representation, mask strategy, and efficiency.

Strong view-aligned object performance and scene-level unseen-region performance are demonstrated. LaRI produces complete, view-aligned point clouds and achieves good overall scene scores on 3D-FRONT.
The limitations and impact statement are written honestly, discussing fixed-layer sparsity, limited observations, and synthetic-to-real domain gaps, which is good research practice.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing for end-to-end geometry. For scene-level evaluation, the paper states it uses the GT mask, which may filter LaRI's predictions with oracle valid-intersection masks rather than its predicted stopping index. The paper should report reconstruction accuracy using predicted masks and quantify the drop. Table 7 only evaluates mask quality, not downstream 3D reconstruction impact.

Real-world unseen-geometry generalization is weakly established. Large-scale training and evaluation are mostly synthetic (Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, GSO), while real-world evaluation is limited to SCRREAM and ScanNet++ (with incomplete unseen regions, mainly used for visualization). More in-the-wild cross-domain testing is needed.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the layered representation is adapted from layered depth images in computer graphics, and the main new component is the ray-stopping index plus supervised dataset/benchmark construction. Comparisons against existing layered-depth or LDI-style geometry methods are limited, so the advance over prior representations is not fully isolated.

Some claims overstate the results. On SCRREAM, overall F-score@0.05 is lower than MoGe (0.590 vs. 0.668) despite better Chamfer distance; canonical object-level results are slightly worse than TRELLIS; and the 'unified' claim is weakened by separately trained object and scene models.

Presentation and reference issues reduce clarity: Table 6 duplicates the 'Ours' rows, Table 6 cites MoGe as Wang et al. (2024a), Table 5 cites DINOv3 as Oquab et al. (2023), and the evaluation masking details are ambiguous.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no code release or random seeds are mentioned, the data generation pipeline is promised rather than provided, and dataset licensing/consent for scanned data is not discussed.

Method limitations are practically important: fixed L=5 layers, lower point density on surfaces parallel to camera rays or between layers, no uncertainty/ambiguity modeling, and deterministic predictions can be inaccurate under limited observation.
